--- title: "What ConvFinQA looks like" --- **You will learn:** - how a ConvFinQA conversation is built from one page of an earnings report; - what the questions, programs and answers look like, for both conversation types; - how big the data is, and how long a full conversation gets in tokens, which sets `max_length` for training. ConvFinQA [@chen2022convfinqa] turns FinQA questions about earnings-report pages into multi-turn conversations. Each page has text before a table, the table, and text after it. A conversation asks a chain of questions about that page, and each turn has a small **program** in a domain-specific language (DSL) that computes the answer. ## Getting the data The code lives in `src/convfinqa/data.py`. The download clones the authors' repository and unzips `data.zip` into `data/raw/`, and does nothing if the data is already there. ::: {#fa8ed03a .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import json from collections import Counter from pathlib import Path import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import pandas as pd from convfinqa import data data.download_data() splits = { name: data.load_split(name) for name in ["train", "dev", "test", "train_turn", "dev_turn"] } pd.DataFrame({ "rows": {k: len(v) for k, v in splits.items()}, "has labels": { k: "annotation" in v[0] and "turn_program" in v[0]["annotation"] for k, v in splits.items() } }) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}
rows has labels
train 3037 True
dev 421 True
test 434 False
train_turn 11104 True
dev_turn 1490 True
``` ::: ::: The official test split has questions but no answers, so **we use `dev` as our test set**. For tuning we carve a validation split out of `train` in a later chapter. The `*_turn` files hold the same conversations unrolled to one row per turn. We work from the conversation files and unroll ourselves, which the counts above confirm gives the same number of turns: ::: {#b88342f7 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} n_turns = { s: sum(len(c["annotation"]["dialogue_break"]) for c in splits[s]) for s in ["train", "dev"] } assert n_turns["train"] == len(splits["train_turn"])\ and n_turns["dev"] == len(splits["dev_turn"]) n_turns ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` {'train': 11104, 'dev': 1490} ``` ::: ::: ## One record A conversation is a JSON object. The fields we use are `pre_text`, `table`, `post_text`, and under `annotation`: `dialogue_break` (the questions), `turn_program`, `exe_ans_list` (the answers) and `qa_split` (see Type II below). ::: {#ed93a51d .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} by_id = {c["id"]: c for c in splits["train"]} conv_I = by_id["Single_AAPL/2002/page_23.pdf-1"] print("Top-level keys of the conversation:") print(sorted(conv_I.keys())) print("Annotation keys of the conversation:") print(sorted(conv_I["annotation"].keys())) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Top-level keys of the conversation: ['annotation', 'filename', 'id', 'post_text', 'pre_text', 'qa', 'table', 'table_ori'] Annotation keys of the conversation: ['amt_post_text', 'amt_pre_text', 'amt_table', 'answer_list', 'dialogue_break', 'dialogue_break_ori', 'exe_ans_list', 'original_program', 'qa_split', 'step_list', 'turn_program', 'turn_program_ori'] ``` ::: ::: ## A Type I conversation Type I conversations decompose **one** FinQA question into a chain of turns. First the page the model sees: the text before the table (shortened here), the table as markdown, and the text after. ::: {#e2b069bd .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} from IPython.display import Markdown def show_page(conv, n=300): pre = " ".join(conv["pre_text"]) post = " ".join(conv["post_text"]) return Markdown( f"*pre_text ({len(conv['pre_text'])} sentences):* …{pre[-n:]}\n\n" + data.table_to_markdown(conv["table"]) + f"\n\n*post_text ({len(conv['post_text'])} sentences):* {post[:n]}…" ) show_page(conv_I) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown execution_count=4} *pre_text (22 sentences):* … declined to 23% ( 23 % ) of net sales in 2001 from 27% ( 27 % ) in 2000 . this decline resulted primarily from gross margin of negative 2% ( 2 % ) experienced during the first quarter of 2001 compared to 26% ( 26 % ) gross margin for the same quarter in 2000 . in addition to lower than normal net . | | 2002 | 2001 | 2000 | |---|---|---|---| | net sales | $ 5742 | $ 5363 | $ 7983 | | cost of sales | 4139 | 4128 | 5817 | | gross margin | $ 1603 | $ 1235 | $ 2166 | | gross margin percentage | 28% ( 28 % ) | 23% ( 23 % ) | 27% ( 27 % ) | *post_text (1 sentences):* .… ::: ::: Then the conversation, one turn per line: question, gold program, and the number the program computes. ::: {#e39eae38 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(data.format_conversation(conv_I)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Single_AAPL/2002/page_23.pdf-1 (Type I) [1] Q: what was the total of net sales in 2001? program: 5363 answer: 5363 [2] Q: and what was that in 2000? program: 7983 answer: 7983 [3] Q: what was, then, the change in the total of net sales over the year? program: subtract(5363, 7983) answer: -2620 [4] Q: and how much does this change represent in relation to that total in 2000, in percentage? program: subtract(5363, 7983), divide(#0, 7983) answer: -0.3282 ``` ::: ::: The first turns just **select a number** from the table. Later turns compute with them. The last turn restates the full calculation, using `#0` for "the result of step 0" so the program stays self-contained. ## A Type I conversation with a garbled table Not every page is this clean. Here is another Type I conversation, whose table header is garbled in the dataset. ::: {#040be04d .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} conv_garbled = by_id["Single_JKHY/2009/page_28.pdf-3"] show_page(conv_garbled) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown execution_count=6} *pre_text (9 sentences):* …tal requirements . we expect this trend to continue in the future . the company 2019s cash and cash equivalents increased to $ 118251 at june 30 , 2009 from $ 65565 at june 30 , 2008 . the following table summarizes net cash from operating activities in the statement of cash flows : 2009 2008 2007 . | 2008 | year ended june 30 2009 2008 | year ended june 30 2009 2008 | year ended june 30 2009 | |---|---|---|---| | net income | $ 103102 | $ 104222 | $ 104681 | | non-cash expenses | 74397 | 70420 | 56348 | | change in receivables | 21214 | -2913 ( 2913 ) | -28853 ( 28853 ) | | change in deferred revenue | 21943 | 5100 | 24576 | | change in other assets and liabilities | -14068 ( 14068 ) | 4172 | 17495 | | net cash from operating activities | $ 206588 | $ 181001 | $ 174247 | *post_text (15 sentences):* year ended june 30 , cash provided by operations increased $ 25587 to $ 206588 for the fiscal year ended june 30 , 2009 as compared to $ 181001 for the fiscal year ended june 30 , 2008 . this increase is primarily attributable to a decrease in receivables compared to the same period a year ago of $ … ::: ::: ::: {.callout-warning title="The header of this table is garbled in the dataset"} The raw `table_ori` shows what went wrong. The header was split across two rows: ::: {#2c4dc85b .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} for row in conv_garbled["table_ori"][:3]: print(row) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ['', 'Year ended June 30, 2009'] ['2008', '2007'] ['Net income', '$103,102', '$104,222', '$104,681'] ``` ::: ::: Read together, the first two rows are a single header row, `['', 'Year ended June 30, 2009', '2008', '2007']`, whose first label was extracted on a separate line from the other two. The cleaned `table` then built a header from the broken pieces: its columns repeat fragments of "year ended june 30 2009", and the year labels also show up in `pre_text` (the trailing `: 2009 2008 2007 .`). This is how the data ships, not a parsing error of ours. The model must work out that the columns are 2009, 2008 and 2007 from the table and the surrounding text, which is part of the task. ::: ::: {#f4606dff .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(data.format_conversation(conv_garbled)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Single_JKHY/2009/page_28.pdf-3 (Type I) [1] Q: what is the net cash from operating activities in 2009? program: 206588 answer: 206588 [2] Q: what about in 2008? program: 181001 answer: 181001 [3] Q: what is the difference? program: subtract(206588, 181001) answer: 25587 [4] Q: what percentage change does this represent? program: subtract(206588, 181001), divide(#0, 181001) answer: 0.14136 ``` ::: ::: Most tables are clean. The check below counts how many have repeated header cells: ::: {#12898945 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} dup_header = sum( len(set(c["table"][0])) < len(c["table"][0]) for c in splits["train"] ) print( f"{dup_header} of {len(splits['train'])} train tables repeat a header " f"cell ({dup_header / len(splits['train']):.1%})" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 66 of 3037 train tables repeat a header cell (2.2%) ``` ::: ::: ## A Type II conversation Type II conversations merge **two** FinQA questions about the same page. `qa_split` marks which turns belong to which: 0s, then 1s. ::: {#1a0cb231 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} conv_II = next( c for c in splits["train"] if data.conversation_type(c) == "II" and len(c["annotation"]["dialogue_break"]) == 6 ) print(data.format_conversation(conv_II)) print("qa_split:", conv_II["annotation"]["qa_split"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Double_AWK/2013/page_123.pdf (Type II) [1] Q: what is the net valuation allowance as of december 31, 2013? program: subtract(13555, 2979) answer: 10576 (part 1) [2] Q: what is the value of decreases in current period tax positions in 2011? program: 3734 answer: 3734 (part 2) [3] Q: what about in 2012? program: 2059 answer: 2059 (part 2) [4] Q: what is the total for these two years? program: add(3734, 2059) answer: 5793 (part 2) [5] Q: what about if 2013 is included? program: add(3734, 2059), add(#0, 5965) answer: 11758 (part 2) [6] Q: what is the average for three years? program: add(3734, 2059), add(#0, 5965), divide(#1, const_3) answer: 3919.33 (part 2) qa_split: [0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] ``` ::: ::: ## The DSL A program is a comma-separated list of steps, `op(arg, arg)`. A turn that only selects a number has a bare number as its program. The operations are `add`, `subtract`, `multiply`, `divide`, `exp` and `greater`. (The authors' code also lists FinQA's `table_sum`, `table_average`, `table_max` and `table_min`, but no ConvFinQA gold program uses them.) An argument is one of: - a **number literal** copied from the page, such as `206588` or `0.14136`, possibly with a `%` sign, such as `19%`; - a **step reference** `#k`, the result of step *k*; - a **constant** from a fixed list. The chapter on the DSL and its executor covers the grammar and the executor in detail. Here we look at what makes an argument a literal or a constant, and how the paper's model decides what it may write. ### Constants The constants are not read from the page. The authors' code defines a fixed list of 18, and every constant in the train and dev programs is in it: ::: {#9a83b01f .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} import re const_use = Counter( c for s in ["train", "dev"] for conv in splits[s] for p in conv["annotation"]["turn_program"] for c in re.findall(r"const_\w+", p) ) assert set(const_use) <= set(data.CONSTANTS) pd.Series( {c: const_use.get(c, 0) for c in data.CONSTANTS}, name="uses (train + dev)" ).to_frame().T ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ```{=html}
const_1 const_2 const_3 const_4 const_5 const_6 const_7 const_8 const_9 const_10 const_100 const_1000 const_10000 const_100000 const_1000000 const_10000000 const_1000000000 const_m1
uses (train + dev) 132 136 138 36 28 14 12 12 18 7 1147 344 0 1 197 0 1 19
``` ::: ::: They are mostly scale factors and counts: `const_100` turns a ratio into a percentage, `const_1000` and `const_1000000` convert units, and small integers such as `const_3` count years for an average (the Type II example above ends with `divide(#1, const_3)`). The rule is by convention, not by whether the digits occur on the page: a number the question needs but does not read from the document is a constant, and the same digits read off the page are a literal. ### Percentages and the executor The official executor (`str_to_num` in the authors' `general_utils.py`) strips commas and tries to read a float. If that fails and the string contains `%`, it removes the sign and divides by 100, so `19%` is evaluated as 0.19. A `const_` token is replaced by its number (`const_m1` is -1). The executor never looks at the page: whether a program may use `19%` at all is decided elsewhere. ### What the paper's decoder may write FinQANet's generator [@chen2022convfinqa] is restricted: at each step it can emit an operator, a constant from the list, a step reference, or a number **copied from its input**. Its input is the question plus the context it is given (supporting text and table rows), split on spaces, and a token counts as a copyable number if, after removing commas, it parses as a number *or ends with `%`*. This is the rule, implemented in `data.copyable_numbers`: ::: {#e3834dce .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} row = " ".join(conv_I["table"][-1]) print(row) print(data.copyable_numbers(row)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` gross margin percentage 28% ( 28 % ) 23% ( 23 % ) 27% ( 27 % ) ['28%', '28', '%', '23%', '23', '%', '27%', '27', '%'] ``` ::: ::: This works because the page text is pre-tokenized: punctuation and symbols are separated from the surrounding text by spaces (`$ 103102`, `june 30 , 2009`, `( 2913 )`), so numbers can be extracted cleanly. The exception is `%`, which the data keeps attached to its number in the first form (`28%`) and also writes as a separate token in the parenthesised form (`( 28 % )`). The attached `28%` is a candidate. In the spaced form, `28` is a candidate and the lone `%` also passes the rule, which looks like an accidental quirk of the check. Whether our own models should be restricted this way is a separate question, taken up in the constrained-decoding chapter. ## How big is it? ::: {#16d0ecf6 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} rows = [] for split in ["train", "dev"]: for c in splits[split]: for t in data.turns(c): rows.append({ "split": split, "id": c["id"], "type": data.conversation_type(c), "turn": t.index + 1, "number_turn": data.is_number_turn(t.program), "program": t.program }) df = pd.DataFrame(rows) per_conv = df.groupby(["split", "id", "type"]).size()\ .rename("turns").reset_index() summary = per_conv.groupby("split").agg( conversations=("id", "count"), turns=("turns", "sum"), mean_turns=("turns", "mean") ) summary["type II share"] = per_conv.assign(ii=per_conv.type == "II")\ .groupby("split").ii.mean() summary.round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=13} ```{=html}
conversations turns mean_turns type II share
split
dev 421 1490 3.54 0.29
train 3037 11104 3.66 0.31
``` ::: ::: ::: {#7d97129c .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.2)) pivot = per_conv.groupby(["turns", "type"]).size().unstack(fill_value=0) pivot.plot.bar(stacked=True, ax=ax[0], rot=0) ax[0].set( xlabel="turns in conversation", ylabel="conversations", title="Conversation length" ) share = df.groupby("split").number_turn.mean() share.rename("number-selection").to_frame().assign(program=1 - share)\ .plot.bar(stacked=True, ax=ax[1], rot=0) ax[1].set(ylabel="share of turns", title="Turn kind") plt.tight_layout() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Turns per conversation (train + dev) and the share of number-selection vs. program turns.](102_what_convfinqa_files/figure-html/cell-15-output-1.png){width=856 height=297} ::: ::: The DSL operations are counted from the **new step each turn adds**: the last step of its program, since each program repeats the earlier steps. ::: {#6673b926 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} ops = Counter() for p in df[(df.split == "train") & ~df.number_turn].program: ops[data.split_steps(p)[-1].split("(")[0]] += 1 pd.Series(ops).sort_values().plot.barh(figsize=(5, 2.5), xlabel="turns") plt.tight_layout() ops ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=15} ``` Counter({'divide': 3254, 'subtract': 2307, 'add': 1119, 'multiply': 475, 'greater': 36, 'exp': 2}) ``` How often each DSL operation is the new step of a turn (train). ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](102_what_convfinqa_files/figure-html/cell-16-output-2.png){width=473 height=230} ::: ::: ## How long is a conversation in tokens? Training uses one sequence per **full conversation**: the system prompt, the page, and every question and answer. So the longest conversations set the memory we need. Turning a data row into token ids takes three steps: 1. **Row to messages.** Our own choice, in `conversation_messages` (`src/convfinqa/formatting.py`): a system prompt, then the page and the first question as the first user message, then the gold program as the assistant's reply, and so on for every turn. The experiments part extends this module for training. 2. **Messages to one string.** The model's own **chat template**, which ships with its tokenizer. It wraps each message in the special markers that the model was trained with. 3. **String to token ids.** The tokenizer itself. Here is step 2 for the clean Type I conversation from above. The page text and table are cut out so the structure is visible. ::: {#82b2710e .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} from transformers import AutoTokenizer from convfinqa.formatting import conversation_messages tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507") text = tok.apply_chat_template(conversation_messages(conv_I), tokenize=False) cut = text.index("\n\nQuestion:") print(text[:260] + "\n[... page text and table omitted ...]" + text[cut:]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` <|im_start|>system Answer with a program in the ConvFinQA DSL.<|im_end|> <|im_start|>user in a new business model such as the retail segment is inherently risky , particularly in light of the significant investment involved , the current economic climate , and [... page text and table omitted ...] Question: what was the total of net sales in 2001?<|im_end|> <|im_start|>assistant 5363<|im_end|> <|im_start|>user and what was that in 2000?<|im_end|> <|im_start|>assistant 7983<|im_end|> <|im_start|>user what was, then, the change in the total of net sales over the year?<|im_end|> <|im_start|>assistant subtract(5363, 7983)<|im_end|> <|im_start|>user and how much does this change represent in relation to that total in 2000, in percentage?<|im_end|> <|im_start|>assistant subtract(5363, 7983), divide(#0, 7983)<|im_end|> ``` ::: ::: The `<|im_start|>` and `<|im_end|>` markers delimit each message and carry its role. The model learns to end every answer with `<|im_end|>`, and that token is part of what we train on. ::: {.callout-note title="Which tokenizer, and why it matters"} The ConvFinQA paper doesn't prescribe a tokenizer; it predates our model. We use the tokenizer and chat template of the model we will fine-tune, `Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507`, so that the lengths below are what training will see. The numbers, and the `max_length` we derive from them, belong to this tokenizer and to our formatting. A different base model would give slightly different counts, so check them again before reusing the value. ::: Now we count tokens for every conversation (step 3). `add_special_tokens=False` is needed because the template has already written the special tokens into the string. ::: {#c24832e4 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} def n_tokens(conv): text = tok.apply_chat_template(conversation_messages(conv), tokenize=False) return len(tok(text, add_special_tokens=False)["input_ids"]) lengths = pd.DataFrame([ dict(split=s, tokens=n_tokens(c)) for s in ["train", "dev"] for c in splits[s] ]) lengths.groupby("split").tokens.describe(percentiles=[0.5, 0.9, 0.99, 0.999])\ .round(0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=17} ```{=html}
count mean std min 50% 90% 99% 99.9% max
split
dev 421.0 1129.0 348.0 451.0 1073.0 1553.0 2150.0 2284.0 2291.0
train 3037.0 1161.0 361.0 272.0 1131.0 1573.0 2422.0 3349.0 3460.0
``` ::: ::: ::: {#32ebba26 .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} lengths.groupby("split").tokens.plot.hist( bins=60, alpha=0.6, legend=True, figsize=(6, 3) ) plt.xlabel("tokens in conversation") plt.tight_layout() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Tokens per full conversation.](102_what_convfinqa_files/figure-html/cell-19-output-1.png){width=567 height=278} ::: ::: We pick `max_length` as the longest conversation rounded up to a multiple of 256, so that no training conversation is truncated. Truncating would cut off assistant tokens, which are exactly what the loss is computed on. The value is saved to a file for later chapters, since stages pass data through files. ::: {#3a3cd444 .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} longest = int(lengths.tokens.max()) max_length = -(-longest // 256) * 256 out = Path("../artifacts/processed") out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) (out / "lengths.json").write_text( json.dumps({"longest": longest, "max_length": max_length}) ) print(f"longest conversation: {longest} tokens -> max_length = {max_length}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` longest conversation: 3460 tokens -> max_length = 3584 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note title="Under the hood"} Notice how numbers like `206588` cost one token per digit in this tokenizer. The foundations part looks at tokenization properly. It is one reason the model writes a program and a Python executor does the arithmetic. ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="Further reading"} The ConvFinQA paper [@chen2022convfinqa] describes how the conversations were built and annotated. The dataset repository is at . :::
